In July the briefing was a copy-paste block. It was as long as the chat allowed, the operator carried it by hand, and the chair triaged from whatever survived the paste. Three things broke: a long session's block described only its last task and silently dropped a nine-project run from the same conversation; a block that pointed at "the message above" arrived alone; and a briefing the operator never pasted was a landing nobody folded.

The fix has two halves. The **file** is exhaustive and committed, so it cannot be lost and the chair reads it line by line. The **pointer block** is short and fixed-shape, so a machine can parse it and a human can glance at it, and it names the file and the exact command that reads it.

## The eleven sections

Every briefing has all eleven, in this order, with the number in the heading. `NONE` where a section genuinely has nothing; never omitted.

1. **Intent against what happened.** What was asked (the prompt's words), what was done, and the divergence named honestly: over-scope, under-scope, a pivot, wasted cycles, or "matched cleanly." A table works well: one row per item of the prompt's work list.
2. **State at close.** Branch, pull request and its state, the squash sha, the deploy and its verification, the live route probed, tests, the walk, the commits, metered spend, local processes stopped, and the effort line (below).
3. **What shipped and the decisive facts.** What landed; the numbers that drove decisions; the research pass with every source and its date; **verified against assumed**, named per claim.
4. **Misses and lessons.** The session's own, honest: a rail crossed, a wrong assumption, a tool that lied, a wasted hour. `None` if clean, and it rarely is.
5. **Opportunities noticed and not taken.** Each a bullet, none built. Time-sensitive ones flagged.
6. **Roadmap position.** Where this sits in its arc, the immediate next step, what comes after.
7. **Needs the operator.** Each question in full: what it is in plain words, what is wrong today, what will be done on each answer, the recommendation with one reason, the alternative, what answering unlocks; and **the best guess recorded in the operator's absence**, with what was and was not done on that guess. Every sentence whose subject is the operator carries its receipt (the drop file and line) or reads "not verified."
8. **Owed and deferred.** Bullets, each with the trigger that should resurface it.
9. **Recommendation.** What should happen next with this arc, ranked, one line of why each.
10. **Contracts, and what this session started.** Contracts produced (exact names and values another arc builds against, copy-paste ready) and consumed; the table of every process this session started, with its id, its command line, and what stopped it.
11. **Merge target and gate.** The pull request, the target branch, the gate that was passed (tests, the reviewer, the walk, the probe), what deploys and what does not. The reviewer is written down in full: its kind (a fresh agent, never a fork), its model, its tool-use count, its scope echo read against the diff, and every finding with what was done about it.

After the eleven: **the loose-ends table**, one row per line of the prompt's work, rails and close, each tagged done, partial (with the gap named), queued (with where), spun off, or dropped (said so).

## The effort line

Section 2 carries one fixed-shape line filled from the tool's own usage record, so the chair can re-set model and effort defaults on data rather than opinion:

```
EFFORT | <session kind> | model <m> | effort <e> | session <id> | started <iso> | tokens_input <n> | tokens_output <n> | cache_read <n> | cache_write <n> | reviewer_findings <n> | subagents <n> | metered_spend $<n>
```

On the estate that wrote this, the line fed a running experiment comparing two effort levels on matched pairs of sessions; chapter 9 has the shape. The model on the line is the id the session actually ran on, read from its usage record, never the alias it was launched with (an alias moves when a new model lands). When the numbers come from a table the session reads, it prints the table's column names first and fills the line from them, so a renamed column fails loudly instead of filling the line with the wrong number.

## The completeness gate

Before writing, the session re-reads the conversation from its first message and enumerates every request; builds the inventory from `git log <start>..HEAD` (every commit and changed file accounted for), not from memory; supersets any interim briefing it emitted; and answers, explicitly, "does this cover every request and every commit from the start?" Recency bias is the named failure mode, and the nine-project loss is why the gate is mechanical.

## The pointer block

Fixed bookends, fixed lines, delivered inside a code fence, emitted exactly once, after the push is verified. `NONE` where a line does not apply. It must locate and validate the work even if nothing else survives: the file path, the ref and sha it was pushed at, the literal `READ:` command, the verdict, the facts line, three bullets at most of what shipped, what needs the operator, blockers, contracts, and the one-line next. It never points at chat prose.

```
=== ORCHESTRATOR BRIEFING ===
ARC: <arc> - session <N>
REPO: <repo> | WORKTREE: <path> | BRANCH: <branch>
FILE: <repo-relative briefing path>
PUSHED: <origin/ref> @ <sha7>
READ: git -C <main-checkout> fetch -q && git -C <main-checkout> show <ref>:<file>
VERDICT: <shipped-live | merged-not-deployed | branch-only-unmerged | design-only | blocked>
FACTS: v<X.Y.Z> | PR #<n> <state> | squash <sha7> | deploy <verified|not-verified|n/a>
SHIPPED:
- <plain-English line, three bullets max>
NEEDS OPERATOR: <full question or NONE>
BLOCKERS: <on-fire item or NONE>
CONTRACTS: <NONE | n in file>
NEXT: <one-line recommendation>
FULL DETAIL IS IN THE FILE. Read it line by line before triaging.
=== END BRIEFING ===
```

**The fallback, the only exception:** if the file could not be committed and pushed, the block carries all eleven sections inline with `PUSHED: NOT PUSHED - <reason>. FULL BRIEFING INLINE BELOW`.

## The fold lines: the part of the file the chair folds from

The eleven sections are for a reader. The fold is a set of writes (the landed row, the board line, the owed items, the rows the prompt carried), and a chair that composes those writes from prose composes them differently every time: an owed item reworded, a carried row forgotten, a result line that names a file path the operator cannot open. So the file ends with one fenced block the chair copies from and never rewrites:

```fold-lines
RESULT: Refunds now show on the customer's statement the same day; proven on a test account.
BOARD: payments-s4 landed, refund path synchronous, version 1.8.3 live
EFFORT: model opus, effort high, 74 minutes, 2.1M tokens in, 61K out
FINDINGS: reviewer 3, all fixed before the merge
SPEND: $0
OWED: Refund email copy || the receipt email still says "within 5 days" || the next copy pass on emails || next || operator: answer
CARRY: 3f9a2c1e done: section 3.3
```

- `RESULT`, `BOARD`, `EFFORT`, `FINDINGS` and `SPEND` appear exactly once. `RESULT` is under 200 characters, plain words, no file path: it is the line the operator reads. `BOARD` carries no pipe character, because it lands in a table.
- One `OWED` line per deferred item, five fields split by `||`: the title, the detail, the trigger that resurfaces it, the band (`now`, `next`, `later` or `someday`), and the owner. The owner is `null` (the chair does it), `operator`, or `operator: <reason>` with one of six reasons only the operator can act on: `answer`, `sign_in`, `send`, `call`, `money`, `in_person`. Anything else is refused, because "on the operator" without one of those reasons is work the chair could do.
- One `CARRY` line per row the dispatch prompt carried: `<id> done: <section>`, `<id> open: <reason>`, or `<id> superseded: <id>`. A carried row with no line is a row that silently stays open forever.

**The check:** [`scripts/fold-lines.py`](../scripts/fold-lines.py) reads the block the way the fold will and prints what the fold would write. The session runs it before the commit; the chair runs it before the fold, with `--carry <id>` for each row the prompt carried.

```
python scripts/fold-lines.py docs/orchestration/briefings/2026-01-15-payments-s4.md --carry 3f9a2c1e
```

Exit 0 prints `FOLD LINES OK` and each write in plain words; exit 1 prints `FOLD LINES REFUSED` and every reason; exit 2 is a file it could not read. Two blocks in one file are refused: the chair would not know which one is the landing. A briefing written before the block existed is folded from the file by hand, as before.

## Two emitters

The session's close emits the briefing as its terminal artifact. The on-demand command `/orchestrator-brief` ([`skills/orchestrator-brief/`](../skills/orchestrator-brief/SKILL.md)) emits the same file and block mid-session when the chair wants a deep status without ending the session, and a `context-dump` mode for capturing a conversation's knowledge before it is closed for good. Same sections, same bookends, same order.

## Forbidden

- Pasting the briefing body into chat when the file pushed.
- Variant bookends. The chair's fold parses the literal ones.
- A rendered question alongside a terminal briefing: a question the session cannot settle lives in section 7 with a best guess, for the chair to surface. A session never ends on a question.
- A briefing that describes only the last task of a long session.
- A starter prompt after the block. Nothing comes after the block.

# 7. Folding from files

*A fold is what the chair does when a session lands: read the briefing file, test that the session is really closed, write the landed row, free the slot, stop the session by id. It is done from the file, never from a paste, and it is done the same minute.*

---

## The landing signal

Two signals, either one starts a fold:

- the session's briefing file appears on the main branch (a merged pull request that added `docs/orchestration/briefings/<date>-<arc>-s<N>.md`, the name the fold check matches against the running table);
- the tool's own session list shows the session as done, and its last output carries the pointer block.

The first is the completion signal proper; the second is the earlier one. The chair watches both: the tick fetches main and lists sessions every hour, and a notification hook (where the tool has one) wakes the chair when a session finishes or needs input.

## The ten-minute fold law, and the check that enforces it

**A fold is owed within ten minutes of the close-out card.** That sounds like a promise; it is written as a check because the promise failed. Notifications and the hourly tick both arrive BETWEEN the chair's turns, so the chair is blind for exactly as long as its longest turn. Measured: a finished session read "running" for twenty-five minutes while the chair answered nine operator messages inside one turn, and in the same window two more sessions closed and a fourth stopped on a network error. Nothing was wrong with any session; the chair simply never looked up.

1. **A chair turn that runs past ten minutes runs the fold check before it takes each new ask**, and handles what it names before the ask.
2. **The fold check is the first step of every tick** (chapter 8) and the first command of any turn a notification opened.
3. **The final message of a turn over ten minutes states the check's result in one line**: "every running session is working", or what was found and what was done about it.
4. **The check is read-only and fast** (seconds, not minutes), so running it too often costs nothing and running it too rarely is the whole failure.

This repository's generic version is [`scripts/fold-check.py`](../scripts/fold-check.py). It reads the queue file's running table and the briefings folder on `origin/main`, and optionally the tool's own session list as JSON, and names every session that owes the chair something: a fold (the briefing landed and the row still holds a slot), a stale row, a folded session still resident, a session that ended without a card, one that needs input, one the tool no longer lists, and one the table does not know about. It also knows the clock: when the running table carries the `Expected` and `Hard stop` columns (chapter 3), a row with no card past its hard stop is named `PAST HARD STOP` with the minutes, and a row past its expected time but inside its hard stop is named `OVER EXPECTED`, so the chair reads its last output before it becomes the first. A cell it cannot read is "could not check", exit 2, never a quiet pass; `--now "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM"` checks against a given clock. It prints "all clear" when nothing is owed, and in that same line names any running row that carries no hard stop, because an all clear about a session nobody bounded is a weaker claim. `python scripts/selftest.py` proves it on a toy repository. Where the tool can run a command on every operator message (a prompt-submit hook), wiring the check into it puts the list in front of the chair at the one moment a signal does reach it mid-turn.

## The close test

Before anything is written, four checks, every time:

1. **The card is up.** The session's last message is a close-out card with a pointer block between the literal bookends. A session whose last message is a progress note or a question has stalled, not landed (chapter 5); the chair answers it, and the fold waits.
2. **The file is readable.** The `READ:` command from the pointer block runs and returns the whole file. When it does not, the read ladder below runs before anyone is asked anything.
3. **The claims hold.** A briefing is a claim, not a fact. The pull request the file names is merged (`gh pr view`), the squash sha is on main, and where a deploy is claimed the live route answers with the new version from the live address. **Merged is not live.** A `200` from a route that answers `200` for anything is not a probe; the probe finds a sentence only the new version has.
4. **What it started is stopped.** Section 10's process table lists what the session started and what stopped each one. The tick's census (chapter 10) confirms it.

## The read ladder

When `READ:` fails, in order, and the operator is asked only at the last rung:

1. `git fetch --all`, retry against `origin/main` and `origin/<branch>`.
2. By the sha on the `PUSHED:` line: the hosting API's contents endpoint with `?ref=<sha7>` (a short sha works, and it resolves after the branch is deleted); then `git show <sha7>:<path>` after a fetch. Never `git fetch origin <sha7>`: fetch-by-sha wants the full 40 characters and the block carries seven.
3. Off disk, in the worktree: `<worktree>/<file>`. An unpushed worktree still has it.
4. `git log --all --diff-filter=A -- "**/<basename>"` for a rename or a move.
5. The other repositories on the machine, for the basename.
6. The hosting API for a repository not cloned locally.
7. Only then: "the briefing file at X is not reachable"; and meanwhile act on the pointer block's `SHIPPED`, `BLOCKERS` and `NEEDS OPERATOR` lines.

## The fold, in order

1. Read the whole file, top to bottom. Section 7 (needs the operator) and section 8 (owed and deferred) twice. Then run [`scripts/fold-lines.py`](../scripts/fold-lines.py) on it, with `--carry <id>` for each row the prompt carried (chapter 6). Steps 3, 5, 6 and 9 copy from the block it prints; they never compose. A refused block goes back to the session (or, if it has stopped, is fixed on main by the chair with the reason in the log line) before anything is written.
2. Act on a non-empty `BLOCKERS:` line before anything else.
3. Write the landed row: the clocks and one plain-English sentence of what changed for the operator, ending with the pull request and version.
4. Free the slot in the running table; move any waiting rows this landing un-gates to READY.
5. Fold section 7 into the operator's open questions, each with its recommendation, linked to its own record, never re-asked in chat if already asked once.
6. Fold section 8 into the owed registry with each item's trigger.
7. Lift any contract in section 10 verbatim into the prompts of the arcs that consume it.
8. Fold any `=== CHAIR UPDATE ===` block (a change the session wanted in a shared document it may not edit) into the board or the rules, on main.
9. Write the board's arc line and the dated log line.
10. **Stop the session by id, the same minute** (`claude stop <id>` on Claude Code; the adapters have the rest). A folded session left resident is pure cost: each one keeps its helper processes, its language servers and its shells alive.
11. Fill the freed slot from the top of the waiting table (chapter 3).
12. One line to the operator: `✅ <arc> session N folded: <what changed>.` And, in the same turn, `🚀 <next arc> launched on <model> at <effort> in slot K.`

## The operator's asks, checked by someone who did not do the work

A session's briefing says what it did. That is a claim, written by the one party with every reason to read its own work generously, and the fold above copies it. On the estate that wrote this, the operator found sessions folded as done whose result, opened, did not do what they had asked. So the asks themselves get a ledger and a verifier.

1. **The ask ledger.** Every request the operator makes is one row, in their own words, with what "done" means in their terms and any quantity they named kept as a number ("all 200 sites", never "the sites"). A prompt that carries an ask names its row.
2. **The verifier.** When a session that carried an ask lands, the chair launches one fresh, read-only reviewer per ask. It gets the operator's words and the live surface (the page, the record, the merged code on main), and nothing else: it never opens the session's briefing or final message, and it is never the session that did the work. It returns MET or SHORT, with what it opened and what it saw.
3. **The verdict is checked too.** The chair refuses a verdict that quotes the session's briefing, one that came from the session itself, and one that calls an ask with a quantity done while the count it read is zero.
4. **Only MET resolves.** A `CARRY` line in the fold block is the session's claim. The ask resolves only when the verifier's verdict on the ledger is MET. A SHORT verdict still folds the session (its slot is freed, its owed items filed), and the ask stays open on the chair with the verifier's reason, for the next prompt.
5. **The operator sees the ledger move.** When a turn changed the ledger, the chair's final message carries one line per change, so the operator never has to ask whether a request was really finished.

Use the cheapest reviewer that can open the surface; the work is reading, not writing (chapter 9). A verifier per ask, not per session: one session can carry three asks and finish two.

## Re-sync before every triage

Sessions merge on their own schedule. Before folding anything, the chair fetches main and reads the new commits: a merge with no briefing yet is still a landing to record, and a task another arc already shipped is not dispatched again. **Validate the task is still outstanding before dispatching**; a session's own handoff can be stale by the time it is read.

That validation is a check, not a feeling. Twice in one day on the estate that wrote this, the chair dispatched an owed item whose work main had already done: once all three items had been fixed by two merges before the prompt was written, once four of five. Both sessions spent their first hour rediscovering it. [`scripts/done-on-main.py`](../scripts/done-on-main.py) is the check: given the briefing the item came from (or a start commit), the files it names and its title, it lists every commit on `origin/main` since then that touched those files, and every commit whose subject shares the title's uncommon words (a fix can land in a file the item never named). Exit 0 means nothing moved; exit 1 means read each named commit before writing the prompt. It refuses rather than answer from a failed fetch, and refuses rather than report "clean" when none of the files resolved, because a clean answer from a check that saw nothing is worse than no answer.

## Validate before you relay

A contract lifted from a briefing into a prompt is checked against the live code first (the column exists, the status value is spelled that way, the route answers). A version in a prompt is read from the version file and the tags at write time, never remembered. A path in a prompt exists on the target branch. Three of the last several relays on the estate that wrote this caught a real defect at this step: a taken version, a wrong path, a renamed script.

## What is gated, still

Self-merge is the default; the chair validates after the fact rather than approving before it. Three things stay gated, surfaced to the operator instead of merged by the session: irreversible or destructive production actions, database schema migrations, and a cross-arc conflict the chair's validation turns up. And nobody merges something another arc still needs open.

# 8. The hourly tick

*The tick is the chair's clock. Every hour, whether or not anything landed, the chair runs the same twelve steps in the same order and writes the same census counts and health numbers. A fleet that is only checked when something happens is a fleet that stalls quietly.*

---

## Why a fixed cadence

Landings are event-driven (chapter 7): the chair folds a session the minute its file appears. But three things do not raise events: a session that stopped early and is waiting for nobody; a slot that stayed free because the top waiting row's gate quietly opened; and a process left resident by a session that ended an hour ago. The tick exists for those. It is started from inside the chair's own tool (a recurring prompt where the tool can fire one, or a bounded background wait whose end opens a turn; never a scheduled task or a daemon on the operator's machine; see "What wakes the chair" below) and it costs one short turn an hour.

## The twelve steps

1. **Sync, then the fold check.** `git fetch origin main`; read the commits since the last tick; list the worktrees; run the fold check (chapter 7, [`scripts/fold-check.py`](../scripts/fold-check.py)) and handle what it names before anything else.
2. **List the live sessions** with the tool's own command. Reconcile against the running table: every running row has a live session; every live session has a running row. A mismatch is written down before it is fixed.
3. **Find the stalls.** For each running session, read its state and its last output. Done with a card up: fold it (chapter 7). Idle with no card: read the last line. A provider refusal (a concurrent-session limit, a rate limit) is a plan switch or a re-queue, never a wait. A progress note or a question with the turn ended: answer it the same minute ("carry on; record the question in section 7"). Waiting on a permission nobody can answer: stop it by id, fix the launch shape, re-queue.
4. **Fold the landings** nobody folded: a briefing file on main with no landed row.
5. **Refill the slots.** Re-read the gates on the waiting table (a card answered, an arc landed, a date passed); move the un-gated rows to READY; launch top-first until the cap, each prompt through the prompt check first (chapter 4).
6. **Run the census** (chapter 10): resident sessions, helper processes, orphans. Stop the orphans that pass the four-part proof, by id, and log each. Put the three census counts on the board beside the running table.
7. **Check the shared configuration** the sessions load (the rules, the skills, the hooks), read-only: is it on main, level with the remote, clean. A finding is fixed the same day on a branch with a pull request, never raised with the operator.
8. **Re-read the operator's open questions, and every inbound message.** Anything answered in chat since the last tick is settled on its record the same turn. Anything asked three times moves from chat to the standing list the operator can open at any hour, and is not asked in chat again. Where the operator can also reach the chair through a second channel (a chat bot on their phone, an email alias), every message that came in that way is listed until the chair's own record acknowledges it by id; an item a bot filed on its own is not the chair having read it.
9. **Re-check the standing rails** that have a mechanical test: no scheduled task or startup entry the operator did not name; no session on a long-context model; every running row with a model and effort filled in.
10. **Rewrite the at-a-glance line** in the queue file with the clock.
11. **Commit** the queue file and the board, on main.
12. **One line to the operator, or nothing.** If something changed since the last operator message: one line per change, each opening with its anchor (chapter 11). If nothing changed: nothing. The full picture is sent at most once between two operator messages; the tick never re-sends it.

## What the tick never does

- Ask the operator a question it asked before.
- Launch a row whose gate is open only in the chair's opinion.
- Start anything that outlives the tick on the operator's machine.
- Elevate, or put a window on the screen, to learn something it could read from documentation.
- Kill by image name.

## What wakes the chair

The tick needs something to start it, and on the estate that wrote this the obvious mechanism failed quietly: with the chair running inside an editor extension, a prompt scheduled to fire at a time could not fire while any background task was running, and the chair always had one running. Fifteen due times were recorded; none fired. Check your own tool before relying on its scheduler. Two things did work, and the chair now relies only on them:

- **A background task's end starts a turn.** A long command run in the background (a test suite, a watch loop with a bound) notifies the conversation when it exits, and that notification opens a turn. A chair that wants to look again in twenty minutes starts a bounded wait in the background and is woken by its end.
- **The operator's next message.** Every message runs the fold check first (chapter 7), so a chair that was not woken is caught up the moment anyone speaks to it.

**A bounded wait has a condition and a bound, both written down:** "until the briefing for payments-s4 is on `origin/main`, or 30 minutes", never "until it is done". It polls something the chair can read (a ref on the remote, a file the chair itself writes, the tool's session list), never a file another session is still writing, which can be read half-written. When the bound is reached the wait exits like any other, the chair looks, and the miss is written down rather than waited on again.

## Measuring the tick

Three health numbers the tick writes each hour let the operator see the fleet's health without reading anything else: sessions busy over the cap; the median minutes from a session's card to its fold (three minutes on a well-run estate; forty when the tick is the only thing that folds); and orphan processes found. A weekly script over the tick's own log lists the three worst sessions by idle time before their card, so the dispatch template can be tightened where the stalls actually happen.

# 9. The cost rules

*Every rule here was written after a measured incident. The first two are the incidents; the rest are the rules, each with the number that justifies it.*

---

## Incident one: the fifty-agent sweep

A mechanical task: read 435 markdown files and extract their to-do items into a fixed schema. The workflow spawned fifty helper agents. Every one omitted `model` and `effort`, so every one inherited the session's model, which the operator had switched to the most expensive one minutes earlier.

Measured from the run's own transcripts: 127 million tokens of context moved (21.7 million written to cache, 105.6 million read back), 1.08 million tokens of output, about $430 at that model's list price. The same work on the mid-tier model would have cost about $86; on the small model about $43. The task did not need the top model. Reading a file and filling a schema is small-model work; the intelligence was in the orchestration (what to read, how to merge, what to verify), which is the main loop's job, not the fleet's.

Because the fleet ran through the subscription and not an API key, no invoice arrived; what it consumed was the account's five-hour window and its weekly allowance of the top model, and it stopped all the operator's other work for the day.

## Incident two: many long sessions, each on the long-context variant

Nine days later the same allowance ran out with no fleet involved. About 28 sessions in 33 hours, twenty of them interactive windows, every one on the top model's long-context variant because the machine default was set that way and nothing launched with an explicit `--model` overrode it. 2.86 billion tokens moved; 29 million of output; an average of about 560,000 tokens re-read per assistant turn. A long-context session does not compact at the usual boundary; it grows toward its ceiling and every later turn pays for the whole transcript. Twenty windows doing that for a day is billions of tokens without a single fan-out.

## The rules

### 1. Every launch names its model and its effort

In the command and in the chat line that reports it. A launch without `--model` inherits the machine default, which is a cost decision the operator made for their own window, not for a fleet. A launch without `--effort` inherits the default effort, which on the estate that wrote this was the highest setting, so every background session for a week ran at extra-high effort without anyone choosing it.

The register, by task:

| Task | Model | Effort | Slots |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design direction, mockup galleries, look and feel | the top model | its top effort | two |
| Implementation from a locked design; back-end builds; audits; document sessions | the strong implementation model | high or the top effort (measured, below) | one |
| Judgment that carries the result (a review of money or auth code; a contract) | the strong implementation model | the top effort | one |
| Mechanical extraction, sweeps, fixed-schema reads | the small model, or a local model | low | half |
| Anything the operator named a model or effort for | what they said | as asked | as above |

**The operator's word overrides the register, and stays in force until they say otherwise.** When a new model lands and the operator says "use it for everything", every row above runs on it, the chair's own window included, and the register waits. Write the word down with its date and clock beside the table so the next chair does not "correct" it back.

**An alias is not a model.** A short alias resolves to the newest model in its family on the day of the launch, so "opus" on Monday and "opus" on Friday may be different models with different prices. Read which model id each session actually ran on from its own usage record, and put that id, not the alias, on the effort line (chapter 6).

### 2. The cap is stated in slots, and it is the operator's word

An ordinary session is one slot; a design session on the top model is two. The number is written at the top of the queue file with the date it was set, and it changes only by the operator's word. It moves more than you would expect: on the estate that wrote this it moved more than twenty times in four days, between two slots and thirteen, and each move was quoted with its clock. The cap serves two purposes: cost, and the provider's concurrent-session limit. At the cap, the first refusal from the provider is reported to the operator the same minute rather than retried; a refusal is a plan switch, never a wait.

**Lowering the cap is a wind-down, not a stop.** When the operator lowers the cap below what is running, every running session finishes on its own and is folded as usual; a freed slot is simply not refilled while more than the new cap are busy. Once the count is at the new cap, it holds there and every freed slot is refilled as before. Stopping a working session to meet a new cap wastes the work it has done and is never what "fewer slots" means.

### 3. Never a long-context variant in the background

The long-context variant is for the one chair that genuinely holds the cross-arc map, and even there it is a choice to make out loud. A session should compact and stay cheap. A session that runs longer than about two hours is a cost event of its own; prefer ending it and dispatching a fresh one with a fresh prompt.

### 4. The swarm law

In play the moment more than about three helper agents run at once, whatever spawns them:

- **An explicit model on every agent.** Never let a fleet inherit the session's model.
- **The top models are never the fleet.** They are single-call, hardest-problem models. They may be the narrow tip of a swarm (one synthesis, one adversarial judge) when the judgment genuinely carries the result.
- **Effort is set per stage.** Mechanical stages get `low`; omitted means high on every agent.
- **Say the plan in one line before launching:** "forty readers on the small model at low effort, three mergers on the mid model, one synthesis." If the sentence would embarrass you on the invoice, change it before launching.
- **Size the context, not just the count.** The fifty-agent run's cost was cached context, not output. Narrow the corpus with search tools in the main loop, for free, before spawning readers; do not hand an agent a large file "for context" it will not use.
- **Kill a runaway at once.** A background workflow keeps spending after you have realized the mistake.

### 5. The review at the close is one reviewer

A session that reaches its ship gate and fans out a review armada has multiplied its own cost by the fleet size. "No fleets" in the rails is read as being about research unless the prompt says the review too, so the prompt says the review too.

### 6. Metered APIs only through a client with a cap

A research fan-out once called a scraping actor directly, eleven runs in ninety-five minutes, and hit the account's monthly hard limit; every other feature on that account answered `403` for the rest of the month. Any metered API is called only through the repository's own client with its per-run ceiling and its spend ledger; a dispatch prompt that touches one names the cap per call and the ceiling for the whole session, and the session stops at the ceiling.

### 7. Batch work over your own data never goes through a paid API when a subscription session can do it

Summarizing your own transcripts, classifying your own archive, extracting facts from your own files: the order is a local model, then a cheap open-weight model, then background sessions in batches on the subscription. The same verification code path (quotes checked against the source) guards all three.

### 8. A router is never the mechanism

Pointing a coding tool at a different provider through a gateway loses the tool's prompt caching. On a median implementation session on the estate that wrote this, 88 million of 88.7 million tokens were cache reads; without caching, the "cheaper" model behind the router cost more than the expensive model with its cache intact. When a different model is wanted, it is run by the CLI that supports it natively or called as a tool from inside a session, never by re-pointing the session.

### 9. Measure completion, not tokens

A trial that reports "40 percent fewer tokens" and not "the same task done, reviewed, with the same defect count" proves nothing. A public benchmark (Terminal-Bench 4.0, as read on 2026-09-19) measured a cheaper model resolving 12 percent of tasks for three times the tokens of a stronger model that resolved 54 percent: the cheap model cost more because it could not finish.

### 10. A long-context model in the chair's own window is a choice, stated

The one conversation that holds the cross-arc map may run on a long-context variant, because it genuinely reads more than any session. It is still a cost decision made out loud, re-examined when the chair's turns grow slow or its allowance runs short, and it never spreads to a background session by inheritance: every background launch names its own model (rule 1).

## The effort experiment

The default effort is re-set on data, not on opinion. The shape: two sessions of about the same kind (research and measure; an audit; a sweep) launched the same hour on the same model, one at `high` and one at the top effort, neither told to behave differently. At each fold the chair records tokens moved, wall time, the reviewer's findings, metered spend, and defects found later (a wrong fact, a page the chair had to fix, a follow-up session the miss caused). The reading, in plain words: what each level cost, what each produced, and whether the extra bought anything a reader can see. The first pair on the estate that wrote this: same wall time; the top effort moved about 58 percent more context and produced about 44 percent more output; both delivered every asked item and both caught a wrong number of their own before publishing it. Defects found later are still being filled in, and the default has not moved until they are.

The bar for moving it is the operator's, and on that estate it reads: **no savings bought with lower-quality output.** A cheaper setting earns the default only when the matched pairs show the same work done with the same defect count. Until then the default stays at the top effort, and every launch still names it.

# 10. Process hygiene

*What a session starts, a session stops. Measured on one workstation: 708 processes resident, 51 of them orphans holding 1.6 GB, every one a leftover of a coding-agent session that had already ended. Nothing had crashed. The sessions simply never cleaned up, and nobody counted.*

---

## Why this is a rule and not a chore

Coding agents do not reliably reap their children, particularly on Windows: each session spawns its own copy of every stdio tool server it is configured with and disconnects them only at exit, and a session stopped from outside often leaves its shell wrapper and that shell's child running. The upstream issue trackers say so; the reporters' own workaround is a cleanup step at the close. So the cleanup is ours, and it belongs in the close and in the tick, not in a monthly panic.

## The seven laws

1. **Every session kills what it started, before its close-out card.** Preview and development servers, the local back end, headless browsers, test servers, `sleep` and `tail` loops, any background helper. The close is not finished while one of them is running. A session that deliberately leaves something running names it in the briefing and says who stops it.
2. **The chair stops a folded session by id in the same minute it folds it.** A session that has delivered its briefing is done; its process tree is pure cost from that second on. Each one is about seven processes.
3. **The census runs at every tick and its counts go on the board.** Three numbers: resident sessions, tool-server processes, orphans. The census starts nothing, stops nothing and writes nothing, so it is safe to run as often as you like.
4. **Tool servers are scoped per project unless the operator names one global.** A stdio server in the user scope is launched again by every session on the machine, which at six sessions is six copies of everything. A remote HTTP server costs zero local processes and is always the better shape.
5. **NEVER kill by image name.** No `taskkill /IM`, no `Stop-Process -Name`, no `pkill -f`. The operator runs an editor, browsers, chat clients, note-takers and a browser bridge all day, and they share image names with what a session spawns. One session once ran `taskkill /F /IM python.exe` to clean up a single development server and terminated fifteen Python processes machine-wide, including other sessions' work. A process is stopped only by its id, only after its command line and parent chain prove it belongs to a finished session or a dead parent, and every stop is logged with the id, the command line and the proof.
6. **NEVER elevate.** A background session does not put a User Account Control prompt on the operator's screen. Before installing anything, take the path that needs no administrator: a user-scope package, or a release archive unpacked under the user's local programs folder with its published checksum verified. When a tool genuinely cannot be installed without elevation, the session stops, does not run the command, and puts the exact command in its briefing's needs-operator section. Measured: an install that fetched an unsigned installer threw a UAC dialog at the operator in the middle of an evening, from a publisher they had never heard of, with no session on screen to explain it.
7. **NEVER put a window on the operator's screen.** A background session invokes no windowed program. Windows Terminal's `--version` and `--help` open message boxes rather than printing; a session ran both, twice, and three "Help" dialogs with an OK button landed on the operator's desktop while they were in another window. The same class as law 6 for every windowed executable: a terminal, a file manager, `start`, a browser, an installer. The command line of a windowed tool is read from its documentation, never by running it. A session that genuinely needs a window (a signed-in browser, a file dialog) drives the operator's own browser through a bridge and says so in one line, or puts the step in its briefing.

   **A browser build is a window too.** A background session never downloads a new headless browser build (a test framework's `install` command, for instance). The first launch of a new browser binary can put a firewall dialog on the operator's screen, once per binary path: measured, a session's production walk installed a new headless shell late at night and the operator got the dialog with nothing on screen to explain it. A session that needs a browser uses the build already on the machine that its framework version names; if that build is missing, it stops, installs nothing, and puts the exact install command in its briefing for the chair to run in the day, with the operator warned.

   **A script is read, not probed.** A script's flags come from its own argument handling (its argument parser, or the lines that read its arguments), never from running it with `--help`: a script that does not know that flag runs its default action. Measured: `bump patch --help` on a hand-parsed version script was `bump patch`, and cut a second version.

## What counts as proof, before any stop

All four, every time:

- the parent is gone, or the parent chain reaches a process that is gone;
- the command line names a session id the tool's session list does not show, or a working directory no live session is running in;
- the process is at least five minutes old (a `sleep` a minute old belongs to a live session's shell call and exits on its own);
- the command line still matches what the census recorded, so a recycled process id cannot be mistaken for the one that was measured.

Re-verify every id against the live process table immediately before touching it, never against a snapshot taken minutes earlier. A census that flags a live session's helper as an orphan is a bug in the census, and it happened on the first run of the census script the estate that wrote this used (not included here: the census is your own tooling's job, and the four-part proof above is what it must apply).

**A stopped task is not a stopped process.** Stopping a long-running background command by the tool's task id routinely leaves the shell wrapper and its child resident on Windows. After stopping any such command, read the process table before believing it: two test runs stopped by task id were still running twenty minutes later with thousands of CPU-seconds on them, starving the measurement the close was waiting for. And the mirror: a session's children are found by parent chain from the session's own process id, never by a path match on a command line, because a test runner started from a script in a worktree does not carry the worktree's path and the negative proves nothing.

## Large downloads

Anything large (a model, a dataset, an installer over about a gigabyte, a bulk export) is asked about before it is fetched: what it is, how big, where it goes, one line. A background session that wants one puts it in its briefing's needs-operator section instead of pulling it. The destination is the drive the operator named for large files, under a named folder, never the user profile on the system drive.

## Never stopped, whatever the census says

Anything of the operator's own: the editor, the browsers, the chat and meeting clients, the note-takers, the sync clients, the password manager, the browser bridge their browsers launch, and every agent session the tool's own list shows with a process id. When in doubt, leave it and write it down.

## How to apply

- A session's close sequence gets one more line before the card: what did I start, and is it stopped.
- The chair's tick runs the census and puts the three counts on the board beside the running table.
- Adding a tool server is a scope decision, stated out loud: which repositories need it, and would a remote server do instead.
- A new orphan family the census does not recognize gets a role added to your census script rather than a one-off kill.

# 11. The communication standard

*How the chair talks to the operator. The operator reads one window, usually on a phone, usually between other things, and usually only the latest message. Every law here comes from a message that failed that reader.*

---

## The four laws

### 1. Plain English, with jargon paired to its meaning

Every technical term is paired with its plain meaning the first time it appears in a message: "merged the pull request (folded the change into the main codebase)", "rotated the branch (started a fresh line of work off the current main)". Coined system names, phase numbers, badge numbers and internal labels are useless to the operator bare; each carries what it is and what it does for them. A recommendation answers three questions in words a non-engineer reads once: what is it, what does it do for me, why now.

**An ask for approval carries its whole context in the same message:**

- what the thing is, in plain words;
- what is wrong with it today;
- exactly what will be done;
- what changes for the operator afterwards;
- the risk, and how it is reversed;
- how long it takes.

A bare "say the word on X" is the defect, however many times X was explained before, because the operator reads only the latest message.

**An ask that tells the operator to do something carries the artifact itself:** the paste-ready text, the link, the exact command. Never "send the message from item 4".

### 2. The volume cap

A status or triage reply stays under about 250 words. Depth goes into a committed file with a one-line clickable pointer. A message that is formatted beautifully and still huge is still a defect. The carve-outs: "explain this to me" gets full length (still short paragraphs, still lists); durable records (briefings, audits, specifications) stay exhaustive; a safety confirmation before a destructive action beats brevity.

### 3. One ask per message

At most one decision or question for the operator per reply. Everything else queues and is surfaced one at a time, each in a later message, when the earlier one is answered. A mechanical paste is not an ask.

**The shape of the one ask, in this order:**

1. The question.
2. The options and approaches.
3. The recommendation, with one reason.
4. What the answer changes.

Never the recommendation woven into the question, or the options folded into the recommendation: the blended form reads as jumbled.

**Where the answer happens.** When the chair's setup has one, the ask points at a **decision card**: one record holding the question, its options and the recommendation, which the operator answers in one step (an issue with a checklist, a form, a document with a reply box). The card is the record; the message links it.

### 4. The mechanical form

- **Headings** on any reply covering more than one topic.
- **No paragraph over two lines.** Three lines becomes a list. Density comes from structure, never prose.
- **Real bullets**, one idea per line. Never hyphens inside a sentence doing a bullet's job.
- **Numbered lists** whenever order or priority matters.
- **More than one item on one line is the defect.** No mid-dot chains, no comma-run lists, no inline-numbered runs, **no semicolon paragraphs.** A long list goes to a file, one item per line there too; it is never compressed onto fewer lines. "What is running and what is queued" is a heading each, then one numbered line per item.
- **Bare labels are the same defect.** Every queue line, reminder and ask carries a full plain-English sentence: what it is and what is being asked, even on a repeat.
- **Bold the crux**, then bullet the content. Never a bold lead-in followed by a prose block.
- **The pre-send gate** runs last on every reply: any paragraph over two lines; a topic change without a heading; a fake bullet; an announce-first or recap-last sentence (deleted). The first and last lines alone must say what happened and what to do next.

## Who is waiting on whom: the ownership law

Every line that names a piece of work says who moves it next, in one of two phrases, never implied:

- **"On me"**: the chair or a session does it, and the line says WHEN ("I launch it into the next free slot", "at the session's landing", "tonight"). Never "the next session to launch", "its prompt is ready" or "queued" bare: those read as if the operator has to start something.
- **"On you"**: only the operator can move it, and the line carries the link and the under-two-minute action.

## The anchor emoji set

One meaning each, at the start of the heading or line it governs, the same in every message, so the eye lands without reading. Nothing decorative outside the set.

| Anchor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✅ | done and verified: what happened |
| 🤖 | on me: the chair or a session does it, with the when |
| 🫵 | on you: only the operator can move it, with the link and the action |
| ❓ | the one question of the message (question, options, recommendation, what it changes) |
| 💡 | the recommendation |
| 🚀 | launched: a session started, with its model and slot |
| ⏳ | waiting on a session to land; nothing for the operator to do |
| ⚠️ | watch: a caveat, something degraded |
| 🔴 | blocked or failed |
| 📋 | the running and waiting lists |
| 🔗 | a link line |
| 🔟 | the top ten |

The escalation register (🚨 for an emergency, 🔥 for something important that has stalled too long) stays rare and stays its own thing; the anchor set is not escalation.

**One-line turns start with an anchor, and two facts are two lines.** A turn opened by a notification, a tick line, or a progress line between tool calls never opens with a bare word: its first character is the anchor for what it reports, and when it carries more than one fact, each fact is its own line with its own anchor. In a scroll of tool-call names, the anchored line is the one the operator finds.

## Every ask links the record itself

A draft to send links the draft's own address AND the message it answers. A decision card links the card. A file links its path. A page links its exact section. Never the page the record sits on, never "it is in the queue". Sending the operator to a page to find a thing whose direct address exists is the defect.

## The rolling top ten

The chair keeps a ranked list of the ten things that most need the operator, re-ranked at every tick and every fold, each line a full sentence with its link and its under-two-minute action. When the operator asks "what do you need from me", the answer is this list, never a fresh survey. An item asked three times in chat stops living only in chat: it moves to a standing page the operator can open at any hour, and it is not asked in chat again.

## One rolling picture between two operator messages

Turns opened by a notification, a landing, or a tick never leave a fragment. The reply is either one line with nothing new, or the full picture of everything since the operator's last message, updated and self-contained (with any paste block they have not used yet re-included). The operator reads only the latest message; they never stitch fragments up the scroll.

**And the full picture is re-sent at most once while the operator is silent.** After that, every notification-opened turn is one line or nothing; an unanswered question is asked once and then lives in the top ten; a paste block is delivered once and pointed at afterwards; the next full picture waits for the operator's next message or the close-out card. Repetition is the defect, not the cure.

## The ask and the result live in the final message of the turn

A chair's turn is often long: it reads, runs tools, writes a file, runs more tools. Most tools that host a coding agent collapse the text written BETWEEN tool calls among the tool rows, and some show only a plain condensation of it. So an ask written in the middle of a turn, however well formatted, is an ask the operator does not see; and a turn that then ends on "see my question above" points at nothing they can find.

1. **Anything the operator must read, answer or act on is in the LAST message of the turn, whole.** Never between tool calls. If work continues after an ask is written, the ask is written again, whole, as the final message.
2. **Text between tool calls is a progress marker only:** one anchored line per fact ("⏳ reading the queue file"), never a heading, never an ask, never a result the operator needs.
3. **The final message stands alone:** what happened since the operator's last message, what is on the chair, the one ask with its full context, the pointer to the top ten. The operator never scrolls up for a piece of it.
4. **The pre-send gate gains a line:** is every ask and every result of this turn inside this message? If not, restate it here.

## A helper's result is read by the operator

When the chair launches a helper agent or a small background check, the tool often displays that helper's final result to the operator verbatim. A helper told to "report back" writes a paragraph of prose for the chair, and that paragraph lands on the operator's screen. So every helper prompt says: **your final result is displayed to the operator.** It is one anchored line, under about 200 characters, written for the operator: who is speaking in plain words ("the hourly check", never a coined name), what it found, and whether anything is on them ("nothing for you to do" when nothing is). It never carries a local file path, an internal label or a link the operator cannot open. The detail goes in a report file at a path the launch prompt fixes, where the chair reads it and restates what matters.

## Say what you did, never what you are about to do

A turn that says work is happening contains that work. "I'm starting X now" and "I'll go do Y" are banned closers: the turn ends, nothing starts, and the operator believes something is running. The honest forms are "X is done, here is the result" and "X is next; this turn ended before it started". A future intention is never written in the present tense.

A time written into a record comes from the machine clock or the transcript, never from the chair's sense of how long something took. One night's records carried clock labels up to seventy minutes ahead of the machine clock, all written from memory, all corrected from the transcript afterwards.

## Pushing back, unprompted

When the operator states a fact that is wrong, a plan that loses them leverage, or a line they intend to send that contradicts an earlier decision of theirs, the chair says so BEFORE executing: one sharp round with the correction and the recommended alternative, then the operator's decision, then the work. Asked to "push back" or "stress test", the chair gives four parts: the strongest counter-argument, the riskiest assumption, what a sharper operator would do, and one concrete failure scenario. If there is no strong counter, it says so plainly. A decision the operator has already made is settled; executing it is the job, and new facts that create real tension are surfaced once, with a recommendation, for the operator to choose.

## Action-first output

- Lead with the action or verdict; the command, path or link on line one.
- End with ONE concrete next action, under two minutes, whenever anything is open.
- Restate state on multi-step work ("step 3 of 5 done: X. Next: Y").
- Time estimates only for the operator's time, in concrete units; never for the chair's own work.
- Wins in try-it terms ("login works: open /login").
- Multi-topic replies: every section leads with its own bold verdict; an ask is never buried mid-paragraph.
- Starter prompts and paste blocks are delivered as code blocks in chat, every time, never as a link to the file. The file is the record; the fence is the delivery.

## Writing rules

- One spelling convention, applied to everything that reaches the operator, including helper-agent output normalized before delivery.
- No em dashes anywhere, including generated pages and deliverables; a spaced hyphen is fine.
- Full names, never nicknames; a thing is named by its real, unambiguous name every time.
- No buzzwords, no filler preamble, plain punctuation; the reader is intelligent.

## A worked example

The operator asked, an hour ago, for two things and went to lunch. Two sessions landed since, one stalled, and one question is genuinely theirs. The message:

> - ✅ **Onboarding session 2 folded:** the three empty first-run screens now say what is missing and what to do. Walked at phone and desktop width.

Three topics, three headings; one question, shaped question-then-options-then-recommendation-then-what-it-changes; every line anchored; every work line says on me or on you; every ask links its own record; under 250 words; and it is the LAST message of the chair's turn, so nothing in it hides between tool calls.

## Carrying this standard to another project

Every law above is a sentence a model can follow, and a sentence a model can drift from. What keeps the standard applied is the same thing that keeps any rule applied (chapter 13): it lives in one file every session loads, each correction the operator makes is folded into that file the same day with the operator's own words and the date, and the laws with a mechanical test (no em dashes, no paragraph over two lines, a final message that carries the ask) get a check at the moment of sending rather than a louder sentence. The chair's starter prompt in chapter 1 carries the short form.

# 12. Going multi-repo

*Three patterns for when the method outgrows a single repository, and one for when the chair runs alone for hours. The two longer documents this chapter points at are kept from July and revised where the model moved.*

---

## One chair across several repositories

One chair can coordinate arcs across several repositories: it holds the cross-repository map, creates worktrees in each, relays contracts and findings between them, and keeps the cross-cutting knowledge. Each repository still keeps its own board, its own queue rows, its own briefings folder and its own worktree discipline. The chair plans and relays; it does not edit the other repositories' application code. In the background era this is mostly a matter of the queue file's Repo column and the launch command's working directory: a row says which repository, the worktree is a sibling of that repository's main checkout, and the launch happens from there.

## One-directional information walls

Sometimes one chair's world must not be visible to another: separate businesses, separate teams, a client's confidentiality, a partnership where one side's finances never reach the other. The pattern: coordinate ONLY through self-contained relay messages. Each message carries everything the receiving side needs and never references anything from the hidden side. One chair may see everything; each walled chair sees only its own world. When drafting anything that crosses the wall, the test is: *could the receiving side infer the hidden side's existence from this message?* If yes, rewrite it.

A wall is also a publish gate. This repository's own [`scripts/wall-check.py`](../scripts/wall-check.py) is the mechanical form of the test: a list of words that must not appear, kept outside the repository, run over every tracked file, exit 0 at zero hits. The same script, with a different list, checks a client deliverable before it leaves the building.

**A gate run by hand is a gate skipped on the busy day, so the gate runs at the moment of action.** Three places, one script:

- **Before the commit:** [`hooks/pre-commit`](../hooks/pre-commit) runs `wall-check.py --staged`, which reads the staged copy of each added or changed file (what the commit will hold, not what is on disk), and refuses the commit on a hit.
- **On the commit message:** the optional [`hooks/commit-msg`](../hooks/commit-msg) runs `wall-check.py --commit-msg` when a list is configured, because a private name in a message is published the moment the branch is pushed.
- **On what no git hook sees:** a pull request's title and body, a release note, an issue comment. These are published too. Write the text to a file first and run `wall-check.py --text-file <file>` before it is posted.

Both hooks read the list's path from `git config wallcheck.list`, so the list itself never enters the repository. With no list, `pre-commit` still checks the built-in shapes (keys, emails, home paths) and says so; the message check in `commit-msg` runs only when a list is set, so a repository that installed that hook for its trailer rule alone is not changed. A hook that cannot find Python or the script refuses the commit with the reason rather than letting it through unchecked.

Three settings keep the gate usable without a way around it: `git config --add wallcheck.skip '*.lock'` leaves out a path whose content is checksums by design; `git config --add wallcheck.allow 'Jane Doe'` excuses a hit inside that exact phrase (the author's own name, say); `git config wallcheck.builtin false` runs your list alone. git's own revert and cherry-pick lines carry a 40-character id that is not a secret, so the message check masks it; a `Signed-off-by` email is a published email, so it is caught unless allowed. None of these is `--no-verify`, which skips everything.

## The relay protocol

Once two chairs run daily, clipboard relaying breaks: the operator becomes the single point of failure for cross-domain dependencies. The evolved system:

- **Relays are committed files** in known inbound and outbound directories, each self-contained with a standard header (`relay-id`, `handles`, `action-owner`, `expects-reply`).
- **Each chair polls the other's outbox at every tick.** The poll is the delivery guarantee; an operator ping accelerates but is never load-bearing.
- **Acknowledgements carry a terminator,** so two polite chairs do not acknowledge each other forever.
- **A relay that NAMES an action does not ASSIGN it:** execution transfers only through an explicit `action-owner`.

The standing routing rule that fell out of it: work executable by the other chair's domain relays to it the same turn it surfaces, and the operator's own list holds only genuinely human judgment. Full specification: [RELAY-PROTOCOL.md](../RELAY-PROTOCOL.md).

## Running unattended

The chair can run alone for hours (overnight, over a weekend) under hard rails: nothing sent, nothing merged, nothing spent; code fixes held as draft pull requests; one ranked morning report at the end. The July document that describes it, [OVERNIGHT-AUTOPILOT.md](../OVERNIGHT-AUTOPILOT.md), still holds with one revision: in the background era the night's work is dispatched as queue rows with the night's rails written into each prompt, rather than done by the chair itself, and the morning report is the landed table plus the top ten. The learning loop at the end of the night (the lessons appended to a file, the run recorded, at most three mechanical self-edits to the night's own instructions shown in the report) is the part most worth copying.

# 13. Lessons into rules

*Every chapter in this repository is a lesson that became a rule. This chapter is how that happens on purpose rather than by accident: where a lesson is written, when it is promoted, what may never be promoted without the operator, and the one distinction that decides whether the fix is a sentence or a check.*

---

## Why this is its own chapter

A fleet makes the same mistake many times before anyone notices, because each session is new and none of them remembers the last. Section 4 of every briefing (misses and lessons) catches the mistake once. Without a path from there to the rules, the next session repeats it, and the one after, and the chair folds the same lesson every week in slightly different words.

## A lesson is a note about one run; a rule is what the next hundred runs obey

Every repeated procedure the chair relies on (a skill, a command, a checklist, the dispatch template itself) keeps two files beside it:

- **`LESSONS.md`**: one entry per lesson, each with its receipt (the briefing and section it came from), the date, and its class (below).
- **`RUNS.md`**: one line per run: the date, what ran, what it produced, and how many lessons it appended ("none appended" is a line too, with its reason).

At the close, the session re-reads its run against its own claims, appends its lessons, adds its run line, and may make **at most three mechanical self-edits** to the procedure it followed, each a dated delta shown in its briefing. Three is a cap on purpose: a procedure that rewrites itself freely after every run stops being a procedure.

## The promotion rule

The step from lesson to rule is mechanical, so nobody has to decide it:

1. **A lesson that appears in three runs of one procedure is promoted into that procedure's body** by the next session that closes it. It is folded into the step it belongs to, never appended to a growing list of warnings at the end, and the three entries are marked promoted with the date. The promotion counts as one of that run's three self-edits.
2. **A lesson about a RULE goes to the rule, never to the procedure.** If the same miss shows up in three runs of three different procedures, the defect is a rule that is not being applied, and a fourth procedure repeating it in its own words makes the whole thing harder to read, not safer. Write it once in the rule's own file, and put a check at the moment of action.
3. **A lesson that would change a rail, the operator's standing decisions, or what a procedure may do unattended is never promoted by a session.** It becomes a proposal in `LESSONS.md` with its recommendation and what answering it unlocks, and the briefing's section 7 carries it to the operator. A run that wants to change a rail is a run that stops and asks.
4. **Class every miss before promoting it.** Two classes:
   - **MISSING RULE**: nothing said not to. The fix is to write the rule.
   - **RULE NOT APPLIED**: a rule said not to, and it happened anyway. The fix is NEVER another sentence. It is a check at the moment of action: a line in the procedure's own checklist, a lint rule, a hook, a script that refuses.

When most of a procedure's misses are the second class, the honest finding is that the system has an application problem, and more prose makes it worse.

## What "a check at the moment of action" looks like

Every script in this repository is one:

- **The attribution trailer.** A rule said commits carry no AI co-author line. The tools add one by default on every commit, and a rule in memory loses to a default applied every time. The fix was not a louder rule; it was [`hooks/commit-msg`](../hooks/commit-msg), which refuses the commit.
- **The unfolded session.** A rule said fold within ten minutes. A chair deep in a long turn could not see the clock. The fix was [`scripts/fold-check.py`](../scripts/fold-check.py), run before each new ask (chapter 7).
- **The worktree with no hooks.** Nobody forgot a rule; a generated folder was simply absent. The fix was a rotation that ends on a proof, [`scripts/rotate-worktree.py`](../scripts/rotate-worktree.py) (chapter 2).
- **The owed item already done.** A rule said validate before dispatch. The fix was [`scripts/done-on-main.py`](../scripts/done-on-main.py), which reads git instead of memory (chapter 7).
- **The private word in a public file.** A rule said never publish a private name. The fix was [`scripts/wall-check.py`](../scripts/wall-check.py), the publish gate, with its list kept outside the repository. A check someone has to remember to run is still a rule, so it moved into [`hooks/pre-commit`](../hooks/pre-commit) and the commit-message hook, where it runs on every commit without anyone remembering to (chapter 12).
- **The prompt that launched broken.** Rules said every prompt has a definition of done, a hard stop, and no instruction to ask. A prompt copied from an older one carries the older one's gaps, and the chair reads prompts by eye. The fix was [`scripts/prompt-check.py`](../scripts/prompt-check.py), run before every launch (chapter 4).
- **The fold composed from prose.** A rule said fold every owed item and every carried row. A fold composed from eleven sections of prose depends on the chair noticing each item. The fix was the `fold-lines` block at the end of the file and [`scripts/fold-lines.py`](../scripts/fold-lines.py), which reads it the way the fold will (chapter 6).
- **The session nobody bounded.** A rule said every prompt has a hard stop. The chair could not see a running session cross it. The fix was the queue's `Expected` and `Hard stop` columns, read by the fold check (chapter 7).

Each one was proven the same way before it was trusted: a toy case where it must say yes, a toy case where it must say no, and a deliberately broken copy that the test catches ([`scripts/selftest.py`](../scripts/selftest.py)). **A test never seen red is not evidence.** A new check counts only after a copy of the code it guards has been broken on purpose (a condition flipped, a refusal switched off) and the test has failed on that copy. `selftest.py` takes `--scripts-dir`, `--hook` and `--pre-commit` so a broken copy can be tested without touching the real files, and [`scripts/mutation-pass.py`](../scripts/mutation-pass.py) does exactly that for 22 guards, one at a time, and names any the selftest missed.

## No new rule without its check, the same day

A rules folder that grows every week is a sign the estate has an application problem, not a knowledge problem: each new paragraph is one more thing the chair must remember at the moment it is busiest. So a line added to a rule file names, the same day, the check that refuses its miss (a hook, a script, a lint or a test), in one register beside the rules: the rule, the check, and the file the check lives in. When no check can be written yet, the change that added the rule says so and owes the check by name. The register is what an audit reads first: a rule with no check is a rule waiting to be broken.

## Folding the operator's corrections

The operator's corrections are the richest lessons and the easiest to lose. When the operator corrects how the chair works (say, a question they missed because it sat in the middle of a turn), the correction is written into the rule's own file the same day, with the operator's words verbatim and the date, and the fix is classed like any other miss. A correction the operator has to make twice is, by definition, a rule not applied, so the second time it gets a check.
